Keywords: Carbon dioxide Electrocatalyst Electroreduction Cu electrode Hybrid nanofibers
An effective fibrous Cu electrode surface, created using a procedure combining high-temperature annealing and electroreduction, is explored for CO2 reduction to produce useful fuels. The nanostructure of this Cu electrode surface contains a layer of nanofibers or nanofibers surrounded by kernels with 30–100 nm diameters. With a specific surface area as high as 458 cm2 per geometric electrode surface area, this nanostructured electrode is found to have a high activity toward CO2 reduction, indicated by itsmore positive reduction potentials and higher catalytic current density than a smooth Cu electrode. The Faradaic efficiency for HCOO− production is 43%, and the electrode surface remains stable during 19 h of electrolysis — better results than with smooth Cu under identical conditions.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
The key technological challenge in the electrochemical reduction of CO2 into low-carbon fuels is the insufficient performance of electrocatalysts in terms of both catalytic activity and stability [1–4]. Polycrystalline Cu-based materials have been explored as one kind of the unique metal catalysts for CO2 electroreduction studies because of their low cost and chemical robustness compared to Pb and Hg [5–8]. However, the activity of Cu is still insufficient, signaled by its large overpotential (almost 1 V); in addition, a fairly broad mix of major and minor products is formed, including hydrogen, ethylene, and methane [9,10]. Also, Cu electrodes have been found to deactivate rapidly during CO2 reduction, especially in aqueous solutions [6]. To address these issues, nanostructured catalyst materials are very promising candidates as they possess unique properties, such as high specific surface area as well as 1-, 2-, and 3-dimensional structures, which can provide more active sites different from those on the surface of a polycrystalline Cu electrode [5,11–13]. It has been reported that the electrochemical reduction of metal oxides is an efficient route to obtain metal particles with altered surface structures, and that the Faradaic efficiencies for this reaction are strongly affected by the synthesis method and the pretreatment of the copper electrode [5,11–13]. However, the underlying reasons for the influence of the

In this communication, we present a combined thermalelectroreduction approach for preparing hybrid nanostructured Cu electrode surface from Cu oxide film on Cu substrates. The special morphology of such an electrode surface can effectively catalyze CO2 reduction with high selectivity and is stable against the deactivation phenomena that plague bulk metal electrodes.

sections.heading: 2. Experimental
sections.text:
To prepare the Cu nanostructured cathodic electrode surfaces, Cu oxide film was first subjected to a thermal procedure. Cathodic electrodeposition of this film to form nanosphericity-nanofibers was then performed in NaOH or H3PO4 solution using a constant potential method. Typically, square pieces of smooth copper foil (99.99% purity, 10 mm × 10 mm, thickness 0.02 mm), used as the working electrodes, were first cleaned by electropolishing at 4.0 V for 5min in 85% phosphoric acid. The electrodes were then annealed in air at a selected temperature for 12h. In this way, the Cu oxide film, containing a mixture of CuO and Cu2O, was formed on the Cu foil surface as shown in Fig. 1A. The electrodes were further electrochemically reduced by applying a potential of −3.0 V in 1 M NaOH or H3PO4 aqueous solution for 10 min. All of these preparations
were performed in a three-electrode cell vs. Ag/AgCl, and the nanostructured electrode surfaces formed at different annealing temperatures then served as catalysts for CO2 electroreduction.
The catalytic activity of the Cu nanostructured surface for CO2 electroreduction was tested using a conventional three-electrode electrochemical H-type cell, in which a piece of Nafion® 117 membrane (H+ form) was used as a separator. An Ag/AgCl electrode saturated with KCl was the reference electrode, and a Pt foil (99.999% purity, 10 mm × 10 mm) was the counter electrode. An aqueous electrolyte of 0.5M KHCO3was used as themeasurement solution, whichwas bubbled with 1.0 atm CO2 (99.99%) to remove dissolved air before the test. The kinetics and electrocatalytic activity of the Cu working electrodes were measured using cyclic voltammetry at a potential scan rate of 50 mV s−1 from −0.2 V to −1.5 V. For comparison, a smooth Cu foil measured under the same conditions was used as the baseline. Electrolysis for product identification was performed potentiostatically, duringwhich CO2was constantly bubbled into the cell. For CO2-saturated 0.5M KHCO3 solution, the pH was about 7.4, so the calculated CO2 concentration was about 2.2 × 10−2 M, using the equilibrium equation [H+][HCO3−] / [CO2]=10−6.1 for a rough estimation.
XRD patterns were obtained with a Philips PW3830 X-ray diffractometer using Cu-Kα radiation (λ = 0.15406 nm). SEM images were taken using a Zeiss Ultra Plus thermal field emission SEM instrument (Carl Zeiss SMTAG, Germany), coupled with EDX. 1H NMR was employed to quantify the concentration of formate product in aqueous solutions. The NMR data was obtained using a Varian Mercury/VX 400MHz spectrometer with the WET solvent suppression pulse sequence. Sodium 3-(trimethylsilyl) propionate 2,2,3,3-d4 (TSP) was used as the internal standard.

sections.heading: 3. Results and discussion
sections.text:
To test the composition and morphology, a Cu surface generated by annealing Cu foil then reducing it in a 1.0M solution of NaOH or H3PO4 was analyzed using both XRD patterns and SEM images. As shown in Fig. 1B, only three narrow, pure crystalline peaks can be seen, centered at 43.3°, 50.4°, and 74.1°. These peaks correspond to metal Cu (Card No. 04-0836) (111), (200), and (220), respectively. No diffraction peaks corresponding to other phases can be observed, indicating that the Cu oxides produced by the annealing process were all reduced to metallic
copper [19]. Fig. 1C–F shows representative SEM pictures including the cross-section view of the modified Cu electrode surface. Clearly observables are the nanostructured fibrous surfaces but with special morphologies: (i) the nanofibers surrounded by “kernels” with 30–100 nm diameters in the layer when H3PO4 solution was used for pre-electroreduction (Fig. 1C and D), and (ii) only Cu nanofibers with 30–100 nm diameters in the layer when NaOH solution was used (Fig. 1E and F). Normally, during high-temperature annealing in air, both Cu2O and CuO are formed on the Cu surface [17,18]. Based on the literature [13,16–18], we believe that the Fibrous Cu film on the Cu electrode surface is produced by the electroproduction of both Cu2O and CuO. However, as the SEM results show, very different electrode surface morphologies are formed when the preelectroreduction solution is changed from H3PO4 to NaOH.
The surface area of the nanostructured Cu electrode surface was determined by measuring the double layer capacitance in N2-saturated 0.1 M HClO4 [12]. As shown in Fig. 2A, surface cyclic voltammograms (CVs) were recorded on both the smooth Cu surface and the hybrid Cu
nanostructured surface in a potential rangewhere no Faradaic processes occurred. The capacitance, C, can be calculated by the equation C=current density/scan rate [12]. The capacitance values obtained for the electrodes generated using H3PO4 and NaOH pre-electroreduction solutions are 11.9 and 11.7 mF, respectively. Both are much larger than the capacitance, C0, of 26 × 10−3 mF cm−2 measured for the smooth Cu electrode. The real surface areas, S, of the hybrid Cu nanostructured surfaces were then calculated to be 458 and 450 cm2/cm2 (electrode), respectively, using S=C/C0. Fig. 2B shows the CVs of both the smooth Cu surface and the nanostructured Cu surface in CO2-saturated 0.5M KHCO3 solution. To compare the catalytic activity, the CO2 electroreduction potentials at a current density of 10 mA cm−2 are used, which are −1.42 V and−1.08V vs. Ag/AgCl for smooth Cu and the nanostructured Cu electrodes, respectively. A positive shift of 340mV from−1.42V to−1.08V clearly demonstrates the improved catalytic activity for CO2 reduction by using the nano-structured Cu surface. To further confirm the better catalytic performance of the nanostructured surfaces, Fig. 2C shows CVs recorded on these surfaces when the Cu foil has been annealed at 300 °C, 400 °C, 500 °C, or 520 °C for 12 h in each case. One can see that annealing the foil at 500 °C results in the most positive potential for CO2 reduction, indicating that 500 °C is probably the optimal annealing temperature for preparing these electrodes. When the annealing temperature was higher than ~520 °C, the formed hybrid Cu2O–CuO was partially delaminated, resulting in poor CO2 reduction activity. However, when the temperature was 300 °C, the hybrid was too thin to form an active Cu nanostructured surface.
The reaction products in the solutionwere determined and analyzed byNMR. The productwas sampled after applying a constant potential of −0.8V and−1.1V vs. Ag/AgCl in a CO2-saturated electrolyte for 90min. As shown in Fig. 2D, the chemical shift of the hydrogen atom in the CH group in formate (HCOO−) is at ~8.443ppm, while 0ppm is assigned to the resonance of the CH3 group of TSP. The area of an individual peak directly corresponds to the concentration of a specific chemical group. Formate concentration was determined with reference to the peak area of the CH proton in formate with respect to that of the CH3 protons in TSP [20]. A Faradaic efficiency of ~43% for HCOO− production was achieved when H3PO4 solution was used for the pre-electroreduction of annealed Cu foil. In comparison, the Faradaic efficiency of HCOO− productionwas only ~1%when NaOH solutionwas used for the fabrication of electrode. However, in both cases, the NMR detected CH3 and CH2 groups (Fig. 2D(a–c)), indicating that the liquid reduction products contained methanol and ethanol. Note that the nanostructured Cu electrode surface in both cases exhibits almost the same surface area, as discussed above. These results suggest that the different solutions used for pre-electroreduction lead to different surface morphologies, resulting in different selectivity for the final reduction products.
The stability of the hybrid Cu nanostructured surface was tracked using CO2-saturated 0.5 M KHCO3 aqueous solution, performed potentiostatically at a constant potential of−1.0V vs. Ag/AgCl. The current density was recorded as a function of electrolysis time, as shown in Fig. 2E. A striking feature is that no appreciable decay in current density was observed, even after 19h of electrolysis. This excellent stabilitymay be due to the strong synergistic effect arising from the formation of the special hybrid surface nanostructures, which effectively prevent deactivation of the Cu electrode. Compared to the smooth Cu electrode surface, the hybrid Cunanostructured surface shows amuchhigher current during thewholemeasurement period. All of these results indicate that the nanostructured surfaces formed on the Cu electrode enable effective CO2 electroreduction.

sections.heading: 4. Conclusions
sections.text: Nanostructured Cu electrode surfaces were prepared by a combined process of high-temperature annealing and electroreduction. The resulting Cu electrode surface contained a layered nanosphere– nanofiber structure, which led to high activity toward CO2 reduction. A Faradaic efficiency of ~43% for HCOO− production was reached at remarkably low overpotentials, along with relatively long stability. The results confirm that the preparation method described in this paper is an easy, simple, and cost-effective way of fabricating Cu electrodes and has great potential for use in CO2 electroreduction to produce useful low-carbon fuels.
